claim: Bacterial chemotaxis requires large, highly ordered arrays of sensory proteins to mediate signal transduction that controls cell motility.
source: Chemotactic responses in bacteria require large, highly ordered arrays of sensory proteins to mediate the signal transduction that ultimately controls cell motility.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial chemotaxis supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A density map of the core-signaling unit at 11.3 Å resolution was obtained by cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging.
source: Here, we report a novel reconstitution of the array, involving the receptor signaling domain, histidine kinase CheA, and adaptor protein CheW, as well as a density map of the core-signaling unit at 11.3 Å resolution, obtained by cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging.
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the resolution achieved through their experimental methods.

claim: An atomic model of the core array structure was computationally constructed and refined using structural constraints from the density map.
source: Extracting key structural constraints from our density map, we computationally construct and refine an atomic model of the core array structure, exposing novel interfaces between the component proteins.
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational modeling approach used to build the atomic model.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations reveal a distinctive conformational change in CheA.
source: Using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, we further reveal a distinctive conformational change in CheA.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from MD simulations showing conformational changes.

claim: Mutagenesis and chemical cross-linking experiments confirm the importance of the conformational dynamics of CheA for chemotactic function.
source: Mutagenesis and chemical cross-linking experiments confirm the importance of the conformational dynamics of CheA for chemotactic function.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental validation of the computational findings.

claim: Bacterial chemotaxis is a ubiquitous, two-component signal transduction system that allows cells to extract information from environmental chemical gradients.
source: Bacterial chemotaxis is a ubiquitous, two-component signal transduction system that allows cells to extract information from environmental chemical gradients and place themselves within the nutrient-optimal portion of their habitat (Wadhams and Armitage, 2004; Capra and Laub, 2012; Eisenbach, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Each bacterial chemotaxis system uses the histidine kinase CheA and response regulator CheY to set up an intracellular phosphorylation cascade that regulates cell motility.
source: Though the topology and complexity of the protein networks employed in bacterial chemotaxis vary by species, each uses the histidine kinase CheA (component 1) and response regulator CheY (component 2) to set up an intracellular phosphorylation cascade that regulates the motile behavior of the cell (Szurmant and Ordal, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CheA is a multi-domain protein consisting of five separate and functionally distinct domains (P1-P5).
source: CheA, in particular, is a multi-domain protein, consisting of five separate and functionally distinct domains (P1-P5): P1-phosphoryl transfer domain, P2-substrate binding domain, P3-dimerization domain, P4-kinase domain and P5-regulatory domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CheA structure.

claim: Bacteria utilize dedicated chemoreceptors (MCPs) to recognize ambient chemicals and transmit mechanical signals across the cell membrane to affect CheA kinase activity.
source: Specifically, bacteria utilize dedicated chemoreceptors (also known as methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins, MCPs) to recognize ambient chemicals and transmit mechanical signals across the cell membrane to affect CheA kinase activity (Ortega et al., 2013; Parkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The adaptor protein CheW universally participates in the coupling of conformational changes within receptors to kinase regulation.
source: The adaptor protein CheW universally participates in the coupling of conformational changes within receptors to kinase regulation (Szurmant and Ordal, 2004; Liu and Parkinson, 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bacteria have evolved the ability to tune or adapt their chemotactic sensitivity to stimulus intensity, giving rise to short-term molecular memory.
source: Bacteria, moreover, have evolved the ability to tune or adapt their chemotactic sensitivity to stimulus intensity, giving rise to short-term molecular memory and allowing an appropriate system response over wide ranges of chemical concentrations (Hazelbauer and Lai, 2010; Parkinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In E. coli, the adaptation mechanism involves the use of two enzymes, CheR and CheB, which reversibly modify specific residues in the receptor molecules.
source: In the case of the model organism, Escherichia coli, the adaptation mechanism involves the use of two enzymes, CheR and CheB, which reversibly modify specific residues in the receptor molecules (Hazelbauer et al., 2008; Hazelbauer and Lai, 2010; Goy et al., 1977; Ortega et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The tunable control of chemotactic activity requires the assembly of collaborative core-signaling units involving the chemoreceptor trimer of dimers (TOD), CheA dimer and CheW monomer.
source: The tunable control of chemotactic activity requires the assembly of collaborative core-signaling units, involving the chemoreceptor trimer of dimers (TOD) (Amin and Hazelbauer, 2010; Li and Hazelbauer, 2011), CheA dimer and CheW monomer (Li and Hazelbauer, 2011; Falke and Piasta, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Through the formation of large, highly organized clusters known as chemosensory arrays, thousands of core-signaling units establish a network of cooperative interactions that dramatically affect signal transmission and regulation.
source: Through the formation of large, highly organized clusters known as chemosensory arrays, thousands of core-signaling units establish a network of cooperative interactions that dramatically affect signal transmission and regulation and endow the basic two-component chemotaxis infrastructure with heightened information processing and control capabilities (Hazelbauer and Lai, 2010; Falke and Piasta, 2014; Sourjik and Armitage, 2010; Bray et al., 1998; Tu, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Atomic structures of the individual core signaling components have been derived.
source: This progress includes the derivation of atomic structures of the individual core signaling components (Kim and Yokota, 1999; Bilwes et al., 1999; Park et al., 2006; Li et al., 2007; Griswold et al., 2002) and several of their sub-complexes (Park et al., 2006; Li and Bayas, 2013; Briegel et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Key interactions between the core signaling components have been elucidated in soluble multi-protein complexes.
source: as well as the elucidation of key interactions between the core signaling components in soluble multi-protein complexes (Bhatnagar et al., 2010; Vu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012) and in reconstituted, attractant-regulated core complexes (Li and Hazelbauer, 2011; Piasta et al., 2013; Natale et al., 2013; Falke and Piasta, 2014; Li and Hazelbauer, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Chemoreceptor TODs form hexagonal arrays with a 12 nm lattice spacing conserved across several distantly related bacterial species including E. coli and T. maritima.
source: Specifically, chemoreceptor TODs were observed to form hexagonal arrays with a 12 nm lattice spacing conserved across several, distantly related bacterial species including E. coli and T. maritima (Briegel et al., 2009; 2012; 2014a; Liu et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior cryoET studies.

claim: The conservation of hexagonal organization has been demonstrated in non-membrane spanning cytoplasmic chemosensory arrays.
source: The conservation of this hexagonal organization has also been demonstrated in non-membrane spanning cytoplasmic chemosensory arrays (Briegel et al., 2014a; 2014b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Studies using cryoET with sub-tomogram averaging have reported the extended structure of the array to consist of receptor TODs packed in a two-facing-two fashion about kinase-filled and kinase-empty rings.
source: Additionally, studies using cryoET with sub-tomogram averaging, in tandem with crystallographic structures of portions of the core complex, have reported the extended structure of the array to consist of receptor TODs packed in a two-facing-two fashion about kinase-filled and kinase-empty rings (Briegel et al., 2012; 2014b; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Past cellular tomography studies have been limited to discerning only the overall arrangement of the core signaling components due to the thickness of cells and cellular crowding and heterogeneity.
source: However, due to the thickness of the cells as well as cellular crowding and heterogeneity, past cellular tomography studies have been limited to discerning only the overall arrangement of the core signaling components.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of prior methods cited in the manuscript.

claim: The lack of a high-resolution description of the intact and extended chemosensory array structure has hindered the development of a detailed understanding of molecular events occurring within the array during signaling.
source: The lack of a high-resolution description of the intact and extended chemosensory array structure has hindered the development of a detailed understanding of molecular events occurring within the array during signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: A novel reconstitution method yielding ultra-thin monolayer samples of core-signaling complex arrays was developed.
source: In particular, we have developed a novel reconstitution method yielding ultra-thin monolayer samples of core-signaling complex arrays, from which we derived a three-dimensional density map of the reconstituted core-signaling complex at 11.3 Å resolution using cryoET and sub-tomogram classification and averaging.
evidence: The manuscript reports the development of a new experimental method.

claim: The atomic model highlights novel interaction interfaces between the receptor, CheA, and CheW.
source: Our model highlights novel interaction interfaces between the receptor, CheA, and CheW and permits the use of large-scale, all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations (Perilla et al., 2015) to further illuminate the molecular details of a key kinase-signaling event.
evidence: The manuscript reports novel findings from their atomic model.

claim: A Ni2+-NTA lipid containing monolayer system was designed to reconstitute the two-dimensional arrays of signaling complexes for structural analysis.
source: Inspired by the template-directed method to assemble functional signaling complexes on lipid vesicles (Montefusco et al., 2007; Shrout et al., 2003), we designed a Ni2+-NTA lipid containing monolayer system (Taylor et al., 2007; Taylor and Taylor, 1999) to reconstitute the two-dimensional (2D) arrays of signaling complexes for structural analysis.
evidence: The manuscript describes the design of their reconstitution system, inspired by prior methods.

claim: E. coli chemotaxis proteins CheA, CheW, and a His-tagged cytoplasmic signaling domain of the wild-type Tar receptor (TarCF) were expressed and purified to high homogeneity.
source: To this end, we expressed and purified to high homogeneity E. coli chemotaxis proteins: CheA, CheW, and a His-tagged cytoplasmic signaling domain of the wild-type (wt) Tar receptor (TarCF).
evidence: The manuscript reports the experimental procedures for protein preparation.

claim: His-tagged TarCF can be readily incorporated into the Ni2+-NTA lipid monolayers, seen as homogeneous particles in the EM micrographs of negatively stained specimen.
source: His-tagged TarCF can be readily incorporated into the Ni2+-NTA lipid monolayers, seen as homogeneous particles in the EM micrographs of negatively stained specimen (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from EM micrographs shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ordered arrays were evident only in the presence of all three components (TarCF, CheA, and CheW).
source: Only in the presence of all three components (TarCF, CheA, and CheW) were ordered arrays evident (Figure 1B)
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Microcrystalline 2D arrays were only formed under strictly constrained input ratios of the three components.
source: and even then, these microcrystalline 2D arrays were only formed under strictly constrained input ratios of the three components, a finding that is consistent with previous results indicating that the chemotactic function of the complex is diminished when one of the components is reduced or over-produced (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental findings consistent with prior work.

claim: The optimal condition for array formation was established to be a mixture of TarCF, CheA and CheW with a molar ratio of 9:18:18 μM in a lipid monolayer containing 2:1 DOPC:DOGS-NTA-Ni2+ lipids (33% Ni2+-NTA lipid).
source: The optimal condition for array formation was established to be a mixture of TarCF, CheA and CheW with a molar ratio of 9:18:18 μM for TarCF:CheA:CheW in a lipid monolayer containing 2:1 DOPC:DOGS-NTA-Ni2+ lipids (33% Ni2+-NTA lipid).
evidence: The manuscript reports the optimized experimental conditions.

claim: The input molar ratio of the reconstitution mixture does not reflect the actual ratio of components incorporated into the monolayer.
source: Notably, the input molar ratio of the reconstitution mixture does not reflect the actual ratio of components incorporated into the monolayer, as illustrated in Figure 1C.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from Figure 1C.

claim: The resulting arrays are organized in hexagonal lattices with 12 nm spacing, resembling the arrays formed in native cells.
source: The resulting arrays are organized in hexagonal lattices with 12 nm spacing (Figure 1B inset, white arrow), resembling the arrays formed in native cells (Briegel et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from Figure 1B and compares them to prior studies.

claim: The reconstituted monolayer system is ideal for high resolution structural analysis of chemosensory arrays by cryoET because the in vitro reconstituted monolayer array is thin (25 nm) and pseudo-crystalline.
source: Compared to previous cellular tomography studies (Briegel et al., 2012; 2014b; Liu et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2007), the reconstituted monolayer system is ideal for high resolution structural analysis of chemosensory arrays by cryoET for several reasons: 1) the in vitro reconstituted monolayer array is thin (25 nm) and pseudo-crystalline, compared to cells with thicknesses ranging from 500 nm to 1 µm
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning for why their system is advantageous.

claim: The monolayer arrays are reconstituted with purified components, hence the system is well-defined, in contrast to native arrays in the crowded cellular environment.
source: 2) the monolayer arrays are reconstituted with purified components, hence the system is well-defined, in contrast to native arrays in the crowded cellular environment
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning for why their system is advantageous.

claim: The reconstituted system allows for control over which array components are present as well as manipulation of their signaling state.
source: 3) the reconstituted system allows for control over which array components are present as well as manipulation of their signaling state
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning for why their system is advantageous.

claim: The in vitro system provides large numbers of sub-tomogram volumes (~3000 core-signaling units/tomogram), thereby improving the noise statistics of the sub-tomogram averaging process.
source: 4) the in vitro system provides large numbers of sub-tomogram volumes (~3000 core-signaling units/tomogram), thereby improving the noise statistics of the sub-tomogram averaging process central to achieving a high resolution structure.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning for why their system is advantageous, with quantitative data.

claim: 20 tomograms of monolayers containing reconstituted core-signaling complex arrays were collected and reconstructed, correcting for the contrast transfer function (CTF) of the microscope.
source: Using cryoET, we collected and reconstructed, correcting for the contrast transfer function (CTF) of the microscope (Fernández et al., 2006), 20 tomograms of monolayers containing reconstituted core-signaling complex arrays.
evidence: The manuscript reports the experimental procedures and data collection.

claim: A typical raw tomographic slice of a reconstituted monolayer shows patches of 2D lattices with information extending beyond 22 Å.
source: Figure 2A (Video 1) shows a typical raw tomographic slice (without CTF correction) of a reconstituted monolayer, illustrating patches of 2D lattices with information extending beyond 22 Å (inset, arrow).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from Figure 2A.

claim: Two major classes of the receptor hexagons were obtained by extracting and classifying CTF-corrected sub-tomograms: one containing a trimer of core-signaling units (CheA2-trimer) and one containing a hexamer of core-signaling units (CheA2-hexamer).
source: By extracting and classifying CTF-corrected sub-tomograms, centered on each hexagon of receptor TODs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, yellow circle), we obtained two major classes of the receptor hexagons: one containing a trimer of core-signaling units (CheA2-trimer, Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, cyan boxes) and one containing a hexamer of core-signaling units (CheA2-hexamer, Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, orange box).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of sub-tomogram classification shown in figures.

claim: The extended lattice organization of the subunits in the monolayer reveals an interlocking of the CheA2-trimer and CheA2-hexamer classes consistent with that seen in cellular tomograms.
source: By mapping the individual sub-tomograms from the above two classes onto the original contributing tomograms, we were able to extract the extended lattice organization of the subunits in the monolayer (Figure 2D), revealing an interlocking of the CheA2-trimer and CheA2-hexamer classes (Figure 2E) consistent with that seen in cellular tomograms (Briegel et al., 2012; 2014b; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from their analysis and compares them to prior studies.

claim: Three CTF-corrected tomograms were obtained from wt E. coli cells that were partially lysed using a phage-gene-induced instant lysis method.
source: To directly compare the lattice organization in our reconstituted monolayer system with that in native E. coli cells, we obtained three CTF-corrected tomograms from wt E. coli cells that were partially lysed, using a phage-gene-induced instant lysis method that we developed recently (Fu et al., 2014), to reduce the sample thickness.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental procedures for native cell imaging.

claim: Extracting and classifying sub-tomograms containing receptor hexagons from the native E. coli cells revealed the same two classes that were observed in the monolayer system.
source: Extracting and classifying sub-tomograms containing receptor hexagons from the native E. coli cells revealed the same two classes that were observed in the monolayer system.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from analysis of native cell data.

claim: The two receptor hexagon classes observed in native E. coli cells formed an interlocking lattice as with the in vitro monolayer system.
source: As with the in vitro monolayer system, the two receptor hexagon classes observed in native E. coli cells also formed an interlocking lattice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from analysis of native cell data shown in figures.

claim: An average density map for the in situ native chemosensory arrays overlapped very well with the map from the monolayer system.
source: Extracting sub-tomograms with an extended unit that contained both the CheA2-trimer and CheA2-hexamer, we obtained an average density map for the in situ native chemosensory arrays that overlapped very well with the map from the monolayer system (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of density maps shown in figures.

claim: The in vitro reconstituted monolayer system with purified E. coli proteins faithfully reproduces the lattice organization found in native E. coli cell membranes.
source: Therefore, the in vitro reconstituted monolayer system with purified E. coli proteins faithfully reproduces the lattice organization found in native E. coli cell membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: The 3D classification process improved the resolution of the class-averaged sub-tomograms of CheA2-trimers to 11.3 Å and CheA2-hexamers to 17.5 Å resolution, as measured by gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC).
source: The 3D classification process further improved the resolution of the class-averaged sub-tomograms of CheA2-trimers (Figure 2B) to 11.3 Å and CheA2-hexamers (Figure 2C) to 17.5 Å resolution, as measured by gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (FSC) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports resolution measurements from their data processing.

claim: A uniform distribution of in-plane orientations of the sub-tomograms and a relatively well sampled, out-of-plane angle enhanced the quality of the averaged density maps.
source: A uniform distribution of in-plane orientations of the sub-tomograms and a relatively well sampled, out-of-plane angle enhanced the quality of the averaged density maps (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B&C).
evidence: The manuscript reports factors contributing to data quality shown in figures.

claim: Some resolution anisotropy exists, with 11 Å in X and Y directions and 15.8 Å in Z direction.
source: Nevertheless, some resolution anisotropy exists, with 11 Å in X and Y directions and 15.8 Å in Z direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports resolution measurements from their data.

claim: The density map was low-pass filtered according to the FSC of the Fourier conical shells along various directions to take the effect of the anisotropic resolution into account.
source: To take the effect of the anisotropic resolution into account, we low-pass filtered the density map according to the FSC of the Fourier conical shells along various directions (Diebolder et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes data processing methods.

claim: The resulting maps of the CheA2-trimer and CheA2-hexamer clearly delineate the density regions corresponding to the receptor, the CheA-P5/CheW ring at the receptor tip, and CheA kinase domain.
source: The resulting maps of the CheA2-trimer and CheA2-hexamer clearly delineate the density regions corresponding to the receptor, the CheA-P5/CheW ring at the receptor tip, and CheA kinase domain (Figure 3B&C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2
evidence: The manuscript reports features visible in the density maps shown in figures.

claim: The individual receptor dimers are thoroughly resolved, allowing the kinase and CheW/receptor interactions to be isolated to a specific receptor dimer.
source: In particular, the individual receptor dimers are thoroughly resolved, allowing the kinase and CheW/receptor interactions to be isolated to a specific receptor dimer (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports features visible in the density maps shown in figures.

claim: The position of the previously unobserved four-helix bundle of the CheA-P3 dimerization domain is clearly discerned to run parallel to the receptor and is positioned close to CheW-interacting receptor dimers.
source: Moreover, the position of the previously unobserved four-helix bundle of the CheA-P3 dimerization domain is clearly discerned to run parallel to the receptor and is positioned close to CheW-interacting receptor dimers (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports novel features visible in the density maps shown in figures.

claim: The maps dramatically refine the area of density projecting below the CheA-P5 domain, suggesting that the CheA-P4 kinase domain alone occupies this density region.
source: In addition, our maps dramatically refine the area of density projecting below the CheA-P5 domain, suggesting that the CheA-P4 kinase domain alone occupies this density region (Figure 2B, 3A, and Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports features visible in the density maps and makes an inference about domain assignment.

claim: The CheA-P1 and CheA-P2 domains are not resolved, likely due to their conformational flexibility.
source: The CheA-P1 and CheA-P2 domains, on the other hand, are not resolved, likely due to their conformational flexibility.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of certain domains in the density maps and provides a speculative explanation.

claim: The density map clearly shows a pseudo three-fold symmetry in which the density at the CheA-P5/CheW interface between core-signaling units (interface 2) is considerably weaker than the density at the CheA-P5/CheW interface within core-signaling units (interface 1).
source: Regarding the CheA-P5/CheW ring, our density map clearly shows a pseudo three-fold symmetry (Figure 2B) in which the density at the CheA-P5/CheW interface between core-signaling units (interface 2) is considerably weaker than the density at the CheA-P5/CheW interface within core-signaling units (interface 1) (Figure 3A&C) (Briegel et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports features visible in the density maps shown in figures.

claim: This finding is in contrast to the previously described pseudo six-fold symmetry of the CheA-P5/CheW ring.
source: This finding is in contrast to the previously described pseudo six-fold symmetry of the CheA-P5/CheW ring (Li and Bayas, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript compares their findings to prior work.

claim: The previously described 'empty hexagon' that is surrounded by six CheA-occupied hexagons is not empty, but rather contains a well-ordered continuous ring of densities that were unambiguously assigned to individual CheW monomers.
source: Most importantly, the previously described 'empty hexagon' that is surrounded by six CheA-occupied hexagons (Briegel et al., 2012) is not empty, but rather contains a well-ordered continuous ring of densities (Figure 2C) that we were able to unambiguously assign to individual CheW monomers (Figure 3D&E).
evidence: The manuscript reports novel findings from their density maps shown in figures, contrasting with prior work.

claim: The ring of CheW provides additional interactions that couple neighboring receptor TODs and strengthens the interlocking baseplate.
source: This ring of CheW, as previously speculated (Liu et al., 2012), provides additional interactions that couple neighboring receptor TODs and strengthens the interlocking baseplate.
evidence: The manuscript makes an inference about the functional role of the CheW ring, consistent with prior speculation.

claim: The maps confirm the existence of the CheW ring and establish its participation in the structural foundation responsible for the ultra-stability of the chemosensory array and for the high cooperativity and extraordinary sensitivity measured in chemotaxis responses.
source: Hence, our maps confirm the existence of the CheW ring and establish its participation in the structural foundation responsible for the ultra-stability of the chemosensory array (Liu et al., 2012; Erbse and Falke, 2009) and for the high cooperativity and extraordinary sensitivity measured in chemotaxis responses (Goldman et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript draws conclusions from their data and connects them to prior functional studies.

claim: The resolution of the cryoET data permitted the unambiguous assignment of distinct regions of density to specific protein components.
source: The resolution of our cryoET data permitted the unambiguous assignment of distinct regions of density to specific protein components, enabling the construction of all-atom models of the chemosensory array substructures and extended lattice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes how their data enabled modeling.

claim: Models of the receptor TOD, CheA-P3P4 dimer, CheA-P5/CheW ring, and CheW-only ring were constructed taking advantage of existing high-resolution X-ray structures from Thermotoga maritima.
source: Briefly, we first constructed models of the receptor TOD, CheA-P3P4 dimer, CheA-P5/CheW ring, and CheW-only ring, taking advantage of existing high-resolution X-ray structures from the thermophilic bacterium Thermotoga maritima (Kim and Yokota, 1999; Bilwes et al., 1999; Park et al., 2006; Li and Bayas, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes their modeling approach using prior structural data.

claim: The component models were heuristically-arranged using a 12 nm lattice constant to produce models of the CheA2-trimer and CheA2-hexamer subunits.
source: We then heuristically-arranged, using a 12 nm lattice constant, the resulting component models to produce models of the CheA2-trimer and CheA2-hexamer subunits identified by sub-tomogram classification (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D&E).
evidence: The manuscript describes their modeling approach.

claim: A dual MD-based strategy was adopted to refine the key protein-protein interfaces within the atomic models, utilizing both unbiased MD and electron-density-biased molecular dynamics flexible fitting (MDFF) simulations.
source: To further refine the key protein-protein interfaces within our atomic models, we adopted a dual MD-based strategy, utilizing both unbiased MD and electron-density-biased molecular dynamics flexible fitting (MDFF) simulations (Trabuco et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript describes their computational refinement approach.

claim: A portion corresponding to the array unit cell was extracted from the CheA2-hexamer model for unbiased refinement simulations, including six receptor TODs, three CheA dimers, and 12 CheW monomers arranged as three coupled core-signaling units.
source: For the subject of our unbiased refinement simulations, we extracted from the CheA2-hexamer model a portion corresponding to the array unit cell, including six receptor TODs, three CheA dimers, and 12 CheW monomers all together arranged as three coupled core-signaling units (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, herein the 'unit-cell model').
evidence: The manuscript describes the system used for MD simulations.

claim: Density-biased refinement simulations focused on the CheA2-trimer model, owing to the higher-resolution of its associated density map.
source: For our density-biased refinement simulations, we focused our efforts on the CheA2-trimer model, owing to the higher-resolution of its associated density map, and hence, better resolved MDFF biasing forces.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for their simulation approach.

claim: Rigid-body docking of the CheA-P4 domain was carried out starting from 10,000 random angular orientations and up to 20 Å shifts from the center of the mass, resulting in 23 classes separated by 3° and 3 Å.
source: Because the CheA-P4 density is not as well defined as the other parts of the complex, likely due to its conformational flexibility, we carried out a rigid-body docking of the CheA-P4 domain, starting from 10,000 random angular orientations and up to 20 Å shifts from the center of the mass. This fitting exercise resulted in 23 classes separated by 3° and 3 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), generating a metric for the goodness of fit of the P4 domain positioning.
evidence: The manuscript describes their docking procedure and results.

claim: The best-fit class of P4 position was chosen for further study based on higher cross-correlation value, higher occupancy, and proper connectivity to P3 and P5 termini.
source: In addition to the class of 'best fit'(Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, panel 1), one other class, in which P4 is flipped relative to the best fit, was seemingly structurally possible (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, panel 5). However, compared to the best-fit class, this alternative class had a lower cross-correlation value, lower occupancy with only a third the number of contributing fits, and the positions of P4-N and C termini are reversed (flipped), making it hard to connect the P3 and P5 termini with short linkers. Thus, we have focused our efforts and resources on the highest ranking class of P4 position.
evidence: The manuscript explains their choice of P4 positioning based on multiple criteria.

claim: Use of the alternative P4 positioning might produce considerably different MD trajectories.
source: It should be noted, though, that use of the alternative P4 positioning might produce considerably different MD trajectories.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of their modeling choice.

claim: Solvation and ionization of the unit cell and CheA2-trimer models produced systems of size 1.25 million and 1.75 million atoms, respectively.
source: Solvation and ionization of the unit cell and CheA2-trimer models produced systems of size 1.25 million and 1.75 million atoms, respectively, which were subsequently energy minimized and equilibrated for 10 ns, as described in the Methods section.
evidence: The manuscript reports the size of their simulation systems.

claim: The unit-cell model was subjected to an 80 ns unconstrained production simulation.
source: The unit-cell model was then subjected to an 80 ns unconstrained production simulation (Video 3)
evidence: The manuscript reports the simulation protocol.

claim: A 70 ns symmetry-constrained MDFF simulation was used to computationally bias the tertiary structure of the protein components within the CheA2-trimer model according to the 11.3 Å CheA2-trimer density map.
source: while a 70 ns symmetry-constrained MDFF simulation was used to computationally bias the tertiary structure of the protein components within the CheA2-trimer model according to our 11.3 Å CheA2-trimer density map (Figure 3, Video 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the simulation protocol.

claim: The resulting unit-cell and CheA2-trimer models agreed well with previous structural studies with respect to the residues participating in the CheA-P5/receptor and CheW/receptor interaction interfaces.
source: The resulting unit-cell and CheA2-trimer models agreed well with previous structural studies, in particular with respect to the residues participating in the CheA-P5/receptor and CheW/receptor interaction interfaces, as defined by NMR (Vu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Ortega et al., 2013), crystallography (Li and Bayas, 2013), and disulfide mapping studies (Piasta et al., 2013; Natale et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript validates their models by comparison to prior studies.

claim: The equilibrated model of the T. maritima TOD maintained the conserved trimer-forming contacts observed in the X-ray structure of the E. coli serine receptor (Tsr).
source: In addition, the equilibrated model of the T. maritima TOD maintained the conserved trimer-forming contacts observed in the X-ray structure of the E. coli serine receptor (Tsr) (Kim and Yokota, 1999)
evidence: The manuscript validates their model by comparison to prior structural data.

claim: The equilibrated model revealed two additional trimer-stabilizing salt bridges, namely E387/R389 (conserved as E402/R404 in E. coli Tsr) and E351/R403 (structurally homologous to D363/R415 in E. coli Tsr).
